title: Cooking for the same family, every day
dek: I thought I would cook the food I decided to make. Then I was making chicken fingers.

body.text: The reason I became a chef at all was because of a Netflix show.

I was a year into a nursing degree, which I had chosen because cooking never registered to me as something you could build a future on at the time. All was going well in the school year, I was enjoying the university days, and nursing never seemed to be too bad. Then one night I watched The Final Table, a Netflix cooking competition show that changed my life. I saw chefs combining flavors in ways I did not know were allowed, specifically burnt flavors. Bitterness is usually described as burnt, distasteful, and does not belong in a dish. And there they were, folding it into something delicious on purpose.
And that is what made me drop out and go to culinary school. The idea that there was that much left to learn.
The belief I had to give up
Before I started, I genuinely thought private cheffing meant I would cook the food I decided to make. My techniques, on my plate, food inspired by me, and a family who would be delighted about it.
Boy was I completely wrong.

Many clients, including mine, like humble food. Some nights that means chicken fingers and fries, not an elevated version with a clever sauce, just chicken fingers and fries because that is what they want.
And at first that was a real ego buster, I do not want to pretend otherwise. There is a period where you feel like the skills you spent years building are going unused, and it stings.

What got me through it was a shift I actually believe now: it is never about what I want. It is always about what the client wants. And once I stopped grieving the plate I was not making, I got a lot better at the job.

There is also this, which took me longer to understand. My internship at Alo taught me exactly how much labor sits underneath a plate that somebody pays a great deal of money for, and I respect that work enormously. But fine dining never gave me a way to connect to food. It is not the kind of food you connect to the way you connect to a meal your grandmother cooked on a Sunday. The food that is comforting and recognizable is what a family comes together for. One that is cooked with love and people bond over it.

That is the food I get to make now. Their favourites like caribbean oxtail, indian goat curry, or even chicken fingers and fries. To me, that is what brings joy and fulfillment to my job. That I get to watch a family share a meal and actually enjoy each other.
I did not choose that as a consolation prize, but instead it was the thing I wanted the whole time.
The 90/10 split
Consistency versus creativity runs about 90/10 for me.
Ninety percent of the time, my clients want food they have already eaten, because it is food they already know they like. If that is what they want, that is what I make.

The ten percent is where I get flare. Something new, fun, creative, that they get to try. Some houses sit closer to 60/40. It genuinely depends on the person, and you will learn your family's ratio within a couple of months.
The dish I have made more times than I can count is Jamaican oxtail and jerk chicken. They love it and request it almost every single week.
There is nothing on that plate that would impress another chef. It is just correct, every time.

So here is how to actually build a house menu. Start with what they already request. Write those dishes down. That list is your ninety percent, and it is more valuable than any concept you could invent. The ten percent is one new thing, introduced once every week or every other week.

You do not need a new tasting menu every day. Trying to force one is one of the most common mistakes I see restaurant chefs make when they transition, and clients read it as the chef performing for him or herself rather than feeding them.
You are building a week, not a dish
A household day for me looks like this.
Breakfast at 9:30 am.
Lunch at 1:30 pm
Snacks and baked goods in between.
Kids' dinner at 6pm
Adults eat at 8pm

More or less it's the same people, same times, every day. Which means provisioning is far lighter than events, because you can actually predict them. That predictability is the gift of household work, so use it. Build a rotation and learn what works for you and the family and what doesn't.

Events are the exact opposite. Every private dinner has a different menu. I plan days ahead, shop the day before, and show up about five hours early. That is where the creative side of my brain gets air, and it is a big part of why I keep 3 days of the week open for private dinners.
Dietary needs are the menu

Dietary complexity is only increasing, and it will keep increasing as people become more health conscious and better informed. Five years ago this would have been simpler with fewer restrictions, less awareness, less action taken around eating well.

Cooking one meal that serves everyone's needs is genuinely difficult. But as a private chef, that difficulty is not an obstacle to the job. It is the job and you have to know how. And the practical version is unglamorous. If two people in a house of five cannot eat the same plate, you are building two plates.

My biggest mistake in year one was trying to figure out how to serve everyone and accommodate all of their dietary restrictions in one meal. Sometimes that worked, but more often, I realized that it was better to make multiple meals or variations.

For example, one person may have a gluten sensitivity while another loves bread and sandwiches. The obvious solution might be to buy gluten free bread, but sometimes the gluten free version simply doesn't taste as good as the original. So instead of compromising the meal for everyone, I might make the sandwich for one person and create something completely different for the other.

When building a household menu, you have to understand that not everything can be substituted one for one.Sometimes the best solution isn't finding a replacement ingredient, it's changing the dish entirely.
This is something I wish I understood earlier. Your job isn't to make everyone eat the same thing, it is to make sure everyone has something they genuinely enjoy and can safely eat.

That means when you're planning your menu, don't just think about recipes. Think about the people you're cooking for, their preferences, their restrictions, and where you may need to create different variations. A good household menu isn't necessarily one menu. Sometimes it's several versions of the same meal, or completely different meals altogether.
Keep developing yourself as a chef

Here is the thing nobody warns you about. You work alone in this job, and your learning can come to a complete halt if you do not deliberately keep it going. There is no chef across the pass showing you something new. Two years can pass, and your technique can be exactly where it was when you started.

I stay on YouTube and I stage in restaurants when I can, specifically to keep the technical side alive. It can be so easy for your techniques to slip away and for your curiosity to fade. Don't let that happen, because the moment you stop learning is the moment you stop growing.

author: Jordan Chan

title: The part restaurants never taught you
dek: Resume gets you the meeting. The hello keeps you in the room.

body.text: When I was transitioning out of restaurants, I felt like an imposter.

I did not think I had the skills yet. I could cook, I had done the sixteen-hour days grinding and building up my discipline as a young chef. But standing at the edge of private cheffing, I was convinced there was some other qualification I was missing.

What I did not understand was that the job is so much more than cooking, and that the extra part is not a qualification at all; clients care about hospitality. How you talk to them, how you handle a situation when it goes wrong. Almost none of that is taught in a restaurant, so of course I did not have it. Neither does anybody else on their first day.

So if you are a restaurant chef reading this and thinking you are not ready, I would ask you to reevaluate. Count what you actually know because it is probably enough to start. The gap is the people part, and the people part is learnable in a way that fifteen years of technique is not.
The first day is not about food
My first day as a private chef was eye opening, and almost none of what surprised me was cooking.
It was the holistic hospitality side of greeting the guest, doing the shopping, managing my own time for prep, managing my own time for cooking, with nobody calling the clock.
In a restaurant, someone else owns the schedule and someone else owns the front door. In a house, you own both, and nobody hands you the keys with an explanation.

I had someone coaching me up side by side, and I am genuinely thankful for it. It took me about two months of doing it daily before I felt like I actually knew what I was doing, and I am certain it would have taken far longer alone. If you can start with a mentor, I would highly recommend it because it has propelled my learning exponentially.

Here is what I would emphasize above everything else: being personable is what decided my hire, more than my cooking history. Clients want to know whether you vibe with their family, whereas your resume gets you the meeting, and the “hello” is what keeps you in the room.
Where to stand
People will tell you a private chef should be invisible. I do not think that is right.
You do not need to be invisible. You need a high enough EQ to understand where you should be, at what time.
If I can hear that a serious conversation is happening between family members, I am not standing next to them. I find something at the other end of the kitchen and I stay there.
But if guests are over, I am not hiding either. I am talking to the guests, making them feel at home, and being hospitable. Disappearing in that moment would be a failure, not discretion.
That is the whole skill. Knowing where you should be and where you should not be, minute to minute.

Discretion is a social skill too, not just a legal one. When a salesperson shows up at the door, I answer it and act like I am the owner of the house, because my job at that moment is to protect my client's identity. Same reflex online: you do not post their faces, you do not post their kids, you ask before any face goes up, and you cover addresses. Every one of those is a small social decision made in their favor.
The tea
If your client drinks tea after lunch, have the water already boiled so they never wait for it.
That is the whole example, and I keep coming back to it because it captures the difference between the two jobs.

Anything your client does not have to think about is something you are quietly carrying for them, and those things accumulate into a feeling that you are indispensable. But restaurants never scheduled you to notice a tea habit. There was a runner for that, or nobody noticed and nobody minded.
In a house, there is no runner. You are the only person in the room who can see it. Which means noticing is now part of your job description.
When the night goes bad
Four extra people show up an hour before dinner.

You can cook for them and that part is fine because you are a chef and you will solve the problem. But dinner is now moving another hour and the grocery number has changed, and the social skill here is saying that out loud. Kindly and immediately, without making it awkward. Extra people come with extra cost.
Silence is how you end up absorbing it, and worse, silence is how you end up blamed for a late dinner that was never your fault.
The worst night I have ever had
I cooked a bag of pasta that contained egg for my client's kids and the kids are allergic to eggs.
It was a random weeknight where I was making food for the kids and I carelessly skimmed over the ingredients list instead of reading it.. Shortly after serving it, they did not feel well.

The clients and I had a conversation about what happened, and I told them the truth, that I had not looked carefully enough at the ingredients. At that moment I thought my job was gone and I fully expected it to be.
But they gave me a second chance, and I am grateful for that in a way that is hard to put into words.

In that conversation I told them how it would never happen again, what I had learned, and exactly what I would do differently going forward. Not excuses but a plan to prevent this from happening again.

What it taught me is bigger than reading labels. Every mess up is yours in this job. There is no team to disappear into. There is no big restaurant name standing behind you to absorb the blame. You take accountability, immediately and completely, because you are the only adult in that kitchen who touched the food.
That is why attention to detail is such an important skill as a private chef. Even the care you take with an ingredients list is the care you are taking with their family.
How you lose the room

I have seen chefs let go for misconduct. Treating the staff and the servers unprofessionally. Partying late and showing up late the next day. A bad attitude that everyone in the house can feel even when nobody names it.
Word of mouth in this industry is fast, and the private world is small.

Nannies, house managers, personal assistants, you are all one operation. If you treat them like they are beneath you, the family hears about it, one way or another, and sometimes even directly. More often it just becomes a feeling in the house that the chef is difficult, and that feeling is very hard to argue with.

So every single time I meet a client, I put on my best self. Walk in with a smile, shake hands, greet everyone in the room, and not only the person paying me. Go above and beyond in a way they can actually notice.
What I would tell you

I want to be careful not to over glamorize this job, because I think that does real damage. My life is better now, genuinely, and by a wide margin. But there are still nights I miss family events. There are still long hours. That is the reality of a service industry, and anybody who tells you private cheffing removes all of it is selling you something.
What it does remove is the part that was breaking us: the pay, the total absence of autonomy, the sense that your passion is being used against you.

Restaurant chefs transitioning into private chef work need to see the whole picture of the industry they are getting themselves into. There is so much more to it than cooking. You need to learn how to communicate, build relationships, create opportunities for yourself, and handle rejection. Practice those skills just as much as you practice your cooking. And most importantly, stay ready so you don't have to get ready, because opportunities will come up and you need to be ready to take them.

author: Jordan Chan

title: Private chef vs. yacht chef vs. personal chef
dek: Pick the lane that matches the life you are actually building.

body.text: Before I tell you about the three lanes, I need to tell you why I picked mine, because the choice is not really about food. It is about the life you are trying to build.

I met my wife two years ago. That is the moment everything changed for me professionally, even though it had nothing to do with a kitchen. I knew I wanted to settle down and I looked at the job I had. Restaurant hours, every single day, long shifts, and I did the math on what that life looks like when there are kids in it. Missing birthdays. Missing school pickups. Being the guy who is always at work.
It was not one breaking point day. It was a gradual understanding of where I was standing and where that road went. And once I saw it clearly I could not unsee it.

So when I chose between the lanes in private cheffing, I chose the one that let me come home. Here is how the three actually break down, so you can choose the one that fits where you are in your life right now.
Where I am, for context

I have been a private chef for about two years, with roughly a year of events and personal chef work layered on top. I am based in Toronto and most of my clients are in the GTA. I do not live in the client’s home, I sleep at my own place and that was non negotiable for me.

I have not done yacht work, and I am not going to write you a fake day on a boat. I will tell you who it suits and what I know about the hire path, and that is where I will stop. Personal chef work, in the version I have seen, looks a lot like fresh in-home meal preparation, packed and ready to be reheated by the client themselves.
Household private chef
This is my lane.

One family, same kitchen every day. Stove, barbecue, pizza oven, the tools are already there and you know where all of them live. Provisioning is predictable because you are feeding the same people, and after a few months you know what runs out on a Thursday.

Here is my actual day. Up and moving around 8am. Grocery store around 9am. Breakfast on the table at the house for 10am. From 10am to 1:30pm I am preparing lunch, making snacks, making baked goods. Lunch at 1:30pm. Then a break, usually a café nearby where I do menus and admin and sit down like a normal person for an hour. Back around 5:30pm for the kids' dinner and adult dinner prep. Adults eat at 8pm. Cleanup is 30 minutes to an hour, and then I drive home.
Hours can run 9am to 9pm when I am covering breakfast, lunch, and dinner. The breaks sit in the middle, which is what makes it survivable. Some clients only want dinner where mine want the whole day.

I will be honest about something here that people do not say enough: household work is more strenuous for me than events. Not physically but emotionally. You are the only one in that kitchen. There is no brigade, nobody to talk to during a long prep block, nobody to laugh with when something goes sideways. It gets lonely at times and in a restaurant the crew is half the reason you survive the shift, and in a house that half is just gone.

That loneliness has a real consequence too. When you work alone, your learning can come to a complete halt if you are not deliberate about it. Nobody is showing you a new technique across the pass. I stay on YouTube and I stage in restaurants when I can. If you take a household job and stop pushing yourself, two years from now your technical ability will be exactly where it is today, and you will feel it.

On paper I have two weeks off a year and I do not take them. I feel an obligation to feed the family, even on days I would like a day off. You should know that the pull exists before you sign up for it.

Pay, if the client employs you directly, is a biweekly paycheck. Some houses come with time off, dental, paid leave, sick pay, holiday pay. Tax comes off the stub, which means you are not doing that math yourself in April.

This lane fits people who want a stable routine and a predictable paycheck. If you like talking to clients and building a real relationship with a family over time, you will like the house. I am in a settled season. I wanted a family and the household job is what makes that possible.
Events and private dinners
Completely different rhythm. Events and private dinners are still up my alley, but I certainly do it less than household private cheffing.

The menu, the logistics, and the team all get planned days ahead. I shop the day before and prep whatever I can prep. On the day, I arrive about five hours early, finish everything on site, and serve when they are ready. Cleanup is the same 30 minutes to an hour.

You figure out the kitchen on the day. You bring your own tools because you cannot assume anything and you adapt constantly. Provisioning is heavier than the house because every single dinner is a new menu.
Events usually need another person, so it feels far less lonely. That matters more than I expected.

You typically charge a day rate or per head. Self employed means you pick the payment method like cash, e-transfer, pay by bill. Contracts can be a single night, or they can stack into something recurring.
If you want creative work and autonomy, you will like dinners more than a house. This is where the ten percent of your brain that still wants to cook something interesting gets to breathe.

I still do them Thursday through Saturday. Monday through Wednesday I am in the house. A lot of chefs stack the two lanes on purpose to make the week pay, and it works as long as you stay on top of your time and do not bury yourself under six clients who all need something on the same Friday.

One warning on the money. The hidden cost of dinners is shopping, planning, and the back and forth messaging with the client. All of that is labor so build it into the price or you will work forty hours and get paid for twelve.
Yacht chef
People who love to travel, do not mind long hours, and want adventure can take yacht cheffing, and they will probably love it.
People with a spouse, a family, and a routine they are trying to protect will hate the demand and the seasons that jump around.

I have never lived in a galley so I will not pretend to describe one. What I know is the hire path is through agencies and your own direct outreach. Yacht work sits in the same high-net-worth world as household and private dining.
If you are trying to settle down, I would not start there. If you are 23 with no dependents and you want to see somewhere, it might be the best decision available to you.
Personal Cheffing

Personal cheffing is a completely different model from working as a household chef. Instead of being employed by one family, you typically work with multiple clients and visit their homes to prepare meals, meal prep, or provide ongoing chef services.

For me, this is where you get a lot more flexibility. You can build your own schedule, choose how many clients you want to take on, and decide what kind of service you want to provide. You might have one client you visit every Monday for their weekly meals, another family you see twice a week, and another client who only books you when they need something.

The trade off is that you are responsible for everything. Finding the clients, communicating with them, planning the menus, shopping, cooking, invoicing, and managing your schedule all fall on you. There is no agency or employer doing that work in the background.

If you want autonomy and the ability to build your own business, personal cheffing can be a great place to start. It gives you the opportunity to build a client base without committing yourself to one household, while also giving you experience with the business side of private cheffing.

The biggest challenge is consistency. You are constantly balancing multiple clients, different dietary restrictions, different kitchens, different schedules, and different expectations. You need strong organization and communication skills to make it work.
For chefs who want to build their own business rather than work for one household, personal cheffing can be one of the best entry points into private cheffing.
What is true in all three
Wherever you land, the boring infrastructure is the same. Food safety, food handlers, smart serve, police check and a contract.

And scope. This is the one that ruins people. Unexpected requests you never agreed to will wreck you in a house, on a boat, or in a cottage. Talk about scope and boundaries before you are already in the middle and too far in to say anything.
How I got in, and how you might
The household job came through Indeed and an agency. The dinners came through my own business where I reached out to people directly, and referrals started to stack from there.

Pick the lane that matches the life you are actually building, not the one that sounds most impressive when you describe it to another chef. I picked household private cheffing because I started a family and I needed a stable income. The yacht can wait. Personal cheffing is there if you want more control and flexibility with your schedule. There is no wrong answer here, there is only the one that fits.

author: Jordan Chan

title: How to build a client list
dek: Text your aunt. Cook the birthday dinner. Write the name down. Ask the next person.

body.text: I never sat down and built a client list. I still do not keep a CRM, and I should.
But my main client list comes from four places: people I already knew, agencies, people who found me online, and people I walked up to and asked.

If you are a restaurant chef waiting for the perfect posting to appear on a job board, I want to take that hope away from you, gently, because it is not coming. The list gets built by you, one name at a time, mostly through slightly uncomfortable conversations at the start.
Start with friends and family
This is the easiest entry point into private cheffing and almost nobody uses it.

Tell the people you already know that you are offering the service. Private events, dinners, celebrations. Ask directly whether anything is coming up that you could cook for. Whether it is a birthday, an anniversary, a holiday dinner.
Then do the first couple dinners at cost, meaning groceries paid for, and labor free.
I know exactly how that sounds. Let me explain why I still recommend it.
That first dinner is not a job, it is an entry point, and it does four things at once.

items: It gets you into the actual work.
It starts your referral network moving.
It gives you your first real credential that is not a restaurant.
It tells you honestly whether you want this life, or whether you just liked the idea of it.

body.text: Some chefs cook one private dinner and realize they hate being alone in a stranger's kitchen. Better to learn that on a free Saturday than after you quit your job.

Through it all, remember to document it. Photograph the food properly, write down what you made, and post it on your social media. That is how you build your personal brand, gather credibility, and credibility is how the next client shows up.
When you feel comfortable in your service you can start to charge. (usually this will take 5 dinners) However, do not let a generous start turn into a habit of working for free.
Key point to remember

It is easier to get your first 5 clients through unpaid work, than it is to get your first 5 clients to pay you. The start of building your client list will be the most difficult, but once the word gets out and the referrals start to come in, you won't be needing to search for more work.
The agency house is one name
My first full time household came through Indeed and an agency. Still to this day, Monday through Wednesday I am working in a household for 5 people.

Think of the agency as exactly what it is: a fast way to get one very good client and learn the job properly. Agencies will match you with families, and they take somewhere around 15 to 30 percent of your first year salary.

Now it is a lot to give up, but what you get in return can be worth it. The duration for household private chefs can vary from a couple months to a couple years, but after a full time placement, I did not need to sign any other client during my time with the household because it paid enough it was worthwhile.
Go where your clients already are
This is the advice I would most want a chef to actually act on, because it is the difference between hoping and hunting.
Get specific about your ideal client. For me that is affluent people living in affluent communities. And what you will soon realize is they cluster in predictable places.
High end gyms, sports car dealerships, private jet companies, luxury real estate agents to name a few.

Get in contact with those businesses, and here is the angle that works: promote your service as a gift they can give their clients. A luxury realtor who just closed a house wants to do something memorable for the buyer. A private jet company wants to add something to the experience. You are not cold pitching a wealthy stranger at that point because you are giving a business owner an easy way to look generous, and they hand you a warm introduction.

Ads work too, for getting your name out. Instagram DMs have booked real dinner parties for me. And again, cold messages land when you use the person's name and spend a couple of minutes on their page first.
What changes after the first house

After about a year into private cheffing for a household, something shifted. People started asking me to cater for their private dinners, birthdays, and special events. I was no longer chasing every single name.
That is when a list starts compounding, and it comes from one thing: one good event throws off a pile of referrals.

Which is why you keep every client satisfied, even the small ones, even the ones who feel like a favor. You do not know who they are talking to at dinner on Saturday. And a bad night talks too, but even faster and to more people.

Two rules I hold to on this. If I cannot take a date, I send it to someone on my team. If I have nobody available, I ask the client to rebook rather than leaving them stranded. A client list dies when you no show, or when you say yes to something you cannot actually handle and then go quiet.
Keeping the list alive
Here is my honest weak spot: I do not actively stay in touch, and it is a hole in my business.

Recurring clients come back so much more easily when something reminds them you exist. What I want to build is a simple CRM. Imagine this, a birthday note that mentions they had a good night last time and asks whether they would like another one. That is all it needs to be and somebody reading this will build it before I do, and they will make money from it.

Be in the rooms too. Facebook groups, Reddit threads, The Brigade community. Other chefs and clients are already sitting in those rooms having conversations, and you cannot get referred from a room you are not in.
Protect the list
Blur the faces. Cover the addresses. Get permission before a face goes up.
Your client list is the most important thing you need to protect, and one breach of confidentiality will come tumbling back down on your business.
Discretion is not a restriction on your marketing. It is the reason the referrals keep coming.
The short version
Restaurant chefs transitioning into private chef work tend to wait for a perfect opening that never posts.
Text your aunt. Cook the birthday dinner. Write the name down. Ask the next person.
That is a client list.

author: Jordan Chan

title: Agency or solo?
dek: Household agencies take 15 to 30 percent of year one. That is the price of the first house.

body.text: My first full-time private chef job came through an agency, and I would not skip it if I had to do it again. But almost everything I have built since then came from finding clients directly.

Both routes can work. They just serve different purposes depending on where you are in your career. Here is how each side actually works, what it costs, and how to decide which one you need right now.
How agencies work
I have worked with one household hospitality agency. There are many of them, and they vary, but the process is fairly standard.

You apply, or occasionally they reach out to you. They want your experience, your resume, and a clear answer to why you want the role. Then comes a call or Zoom, background checks, and verification with past employers. They send your packet to the house and then the family interviews you, or they run a trial.

Household agencies typically take somewhere around 15 to 30 percent of your first year's salary. That is a wide range and it matters enormously, so ask that number before you sign anything. Also ask whether the contract blocks you from working with other agencies, because some do, and finding that out later is an expensive surprise.

One thing worth understanding rather than resenting: agencies want chefs who already have experience. They are protecting their own trust and image with families who pay them well to not make mistakes. When an agency passes on you, they are usually not judging your cooking. They are managing their risk with a client relationship worth more than your placement fee.
What the agency actually gave me
I found the job on Indeed. A chef in Toronto was starting his own agency and decided to take me on, and we worked a family together.
That is the part I want to underline: together. I had someone next to me who had done this before, coaching me up in real time, while I learned what the job actually was.

My first day was eye opening in a way I did not expect. The gap between restaurant chef and private chef was much wider than "cook in a house instead of a restaurant." The whole holistic hospitality side from greeting the guest, shopping managing my own time for prep, managing my own time for cooking, with nobody calling out the clock. All of it was new.

It took me about two months of doing it every single day before I felt like I actually knew what I was doing. A lot of reps and a lot of mistakes to learn from. And I got through those two months much faster because someone was standing beside me.
So my honest advice: if you can start with a mentor, start with a mentor. It will set you up for the rest of your private chef career, and it is worth giving up a percentage for.
That placement was full time, so I did not need the agency again afterward. Most of my work now comes from clients I found myself.
What it costs to go solo
I am based in Canada, here are roughly what my costs looked like when I started:

I went through the CRA site and incorporated, about $200. Food handlers certification, about $50. Payroll and accounting software, about $100 a month. Once people work under you, you need that software and you need contracts for them too. Then insurance once you get bigger.
Admin runs about 1 to 2 hours a week. Menus, schedules, paycheck things. It is not overwhelming, but it is real, and it is time you are not being paid for directly, so account for it in your pricing.

The hardest part of being in business is not the paperwork. It is other people. Paying them well, respecting them, giving them enough information and enough room to grow their own careers instead of just using them as hands for a night.

I feel strongly about this because of where I came from. I watched the restaurant industry take advantage of chefs' passion, pay a couple of dollars over minimum wage for twelve to sixteen hour days, and call it an opportunity.
Which route pays more
I do not think the route decides the pay, instead the client does.

If you are asking who pays well, the answer is high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth individuals who already value private dining, the same pool that hires household chefs, private dinner chefs, and yacht chefs.
Agency gets you into a house faster, if you already have a resume that clears their bar. Less searching, more structure, a real client on day one.

Solo gets you the dinners you go out and ask for. Friends and family, high end gyms, sports car dealerships, luxury real estate agents, and other places where affluent people already spend their time. And the strategy I think is most underused: go where affluent people already are, get in contact with those businesses and promote your service as a gift they can give their own clients.
How I actually run it
I stack the week. House Monday through Wednesday. Private dinners Thursday through Saturday.

The house paycheck is the stable piece, and stability is what I needed when I was building a life with my wife. The dinners are the business I built after I proved to myself I could do it without an agency in the middle. If you were just starting out, I would recommend doing private dinners to get reps and see if this is something you enjoy.

author: Jordan Chan

title: Expenses, reimbursement, and pay
dek: Never eat the grocery cost. Charge for the hours that are not cooking.

body.text: I remember one of my first private dinners where I catered for a dinner party for six people. I worked about five hours and got my payout plus a $200 tip.
I remember standing there afterward doing the math and feeling in shock, because I had just made more in one night than I could have made in a full week in a restaurant.
That is the discrepancy. That is the flaw in the industry we all came up in.

I want to be direct because it is the engine behind everything else in this article. Chefs are taken advantage of because of their passion for cooking. Paying someone a couple of dollars over minimum wage to work twelve to sixteen hour days is robbery, and the only reason restaurants get away with it is that they have found people who love the craft enough to accept it. Being willing to do something out of passion does not justify underpaying you for it.

So when I talk about charging properly, tracking your hours, and getting your grocery money back, I am talking about undoing a habit that the restaurant industry trained into all of us: the habit of not counting our own labor.
Employment vs self-employment

There are really two different financial structures you will encounter as a private chef. If the client employs you directly, you are generally paid through a regular paycheck. If you are self-employed, you invoice the client and decide how you want to collect payment. Cash, e-transfer, or another method.

I am employed on the household job. That comes with paid leave, sick pay, and holiday pay, and tax comes off the stub so I am not doing that math myself in April. It is stable, and stability is exactly what I wanted at this point in my life.
Self employment means you file everything yourself. Holidays and sick days are on you and if you do not work, you do not get paid.

Household chef jobs can come with time off, dental, and other benefits. They can also come with an unspoken expectation that you work when you are sick, because you are the only chef and dinner still has to happen. Depending on your client, there may be no pension, there may be no healthcare, and chefs forget to ask about that part until they are already six months in.
Ask before you sign, not after.
How the food money actually moves
This is the mechanic nobody explains to a new private chef, so here is mine exactly.

I put groceries on my own personal or company, and I get reimbursed at the end of the night. I use my card on purpose so I keep the points, which over a year of feeding a household of six is not a small number.

All my receipts get tracked on notion. I keep a table and at the end of the week I add up the total and send it over to my clients for reimbursement. Reconciliation is a text message with the grocery breakdown attached. It takes just a couple minutes and it removes every possible argument about money before it can start.
The rule underneath the system is simple: you should never eat the grocery cost. Get it back every single time because the moment you absorb it once, it becomes the expectation.
Charge for the hours that are not cooking
This is the biggest money mistake I see, and I made it myself for longer than I should have.
New private chefs bill the cooking window. They count the hours they were standing at the stove and they charge for those, and everything else is invisible.

But shopping, drafting the men, back-and-forth messaging with the client is labor. On a private dinner, all of that can add up to more hours than the service itself, so record every hour and put it in the final price.

I learned this the hard way in my first year. In a restaurant you have support where other chefs hold pieces of the day for you. As a private chef, the cooking, the cleaning, the menu planning, and the grocery shopping all sit on you and nobody tells you how much time each of those tasks deserves. It took me a year to build a real sense of it.
Once you know how long the whole week actually takes, you can finally charge for the whole week.
Put it in writing
The contract is how you stop hoping things will work themselves out.
Get these in there: your pay, how often you work, days off, what the client needs to provide and payment terms.

I do not let reimbursements sit more than a week late. I have been paid late before, and it is a specific kind of stress. You do not want to be the person nagging a wealthy family about money while also cooking their dinner. So now it is written down: payment within one week after the receipts have been sent out.
For pricing an event/dinner party, I look at household size, travel, the type of food, how much food, and whether I need extra labor.
How to set your rate

My rate has gone up over the years, and it went up for a specific reason: my execution went up. More years with more reps and a genuinely more premium service. If you are new, look up chefs at your skill level with your years of experience. That gives you a ballpark for your city so I would start there.

I still aim to charge more over time because it is easier to charge one person more than to charge ten people less for the same work. Ten clients at a low rate is ten times the shopping, ten menus, ten sets of messages, and one exhausted chef.
Starting out, you may not feel comfortable charging what the internet tells you to charge, and that is normal, the money will come with consistency and time.
On underpricing yourself
I have underpriced myself a lot.

Imposter syndrome does that, and the thing about imposter syndrome is that you do not feel it in the moment. In the moment it feels reasonable and not wanting to seem greedy. Then a couple of years later you look back at a number you charged and cannot understand why you charged it.

Sometimes the reason you don't feel confident charging more is because the service genuinely isn't worth more yet. If that's the case, change the reality. Improve your cooking, improve your hospitality, improve your communication, improve your systems, get more experience, build a better portfolio. Then the price becomes easier to defend because the service actually changed.

That said, underpricing is not always a mistake at the very beginning. I tell new private chefs to charge grocery reimbursement and no labor on their first dinner, because they genuinely have no experience in a household yet. That first dinner is school, and you are paying for school with your time.
After you feel more comfortable, you can start to charge your regular rate.
The raise conversation
Informing my clients about a raise in price still makes me uncomfortable. I want to say that plainly, because I do not think discomfort is a sign you should not ask.

What works for me is check ins rather than a single dramatic ask. I talk about how I have improved and how I am adding more value than I was six months ago. That framing is what gets me the yes. I am not asking for more money for the same work, I am telling them the work has changed.
Here is a message I have actually sent, close to word for word:

Hi [name], I wanted to inform you that I'll be raising my prices. I know that we have been working together for a while now, however I have made advancements in my career, and for me to do so I have decided to raise my prices. I hope you understand and we can still work together.
Also worth knowing: money is not the only lever. You can negotiate gas, housing, car insurance, and time off. Sometimes the easier yes is not the hourly rate.

And if you are self-employed, take the tax side seriously and get professional help if you need it. Keep your records, understand your legitimate business expenses, and don't wait until tax season to figure everything out.
Know what you’re actually selling

Charge for the shopping, get the grocery reimbursement back every time, track your expenses so you know what your week actually costs you. And when your skill, experience, and the value of your service genuinely go up, don't be afraid to raise your rate.

The biggest shift is understanding that you are not just selling the hours you spend cooking. You are selling everything that happens before, during, and after the meal. Once you understand what you're actually selling, you can start charging for it properly.

author: Jordan Chan

title: How to network
dek: I stopped at a red light in an affluent neighbourhood and asked. A couple of days later I was cooking for them.

body.text: One day, I was driving through an affluent community, the kind of neighbourhood where the households I wanted to work with actually lived. I stopped, drove up to someone at a red light, and asked if they needed a private chef.
A couple of days later, I was cooking for them.

I lead with that story because "networking" sounds like a conference badge and a LinkedIn message, and in this job, it is almost never that. It is about asking and being willing to put yourself out there while everyone else waits for a job posting.
Where my clients have actually come from

My first clients came from reaching out to friends, family and people on Instagram. The first full time house came through an agency. After that, the network started growing on its own and people came to me for dinners.

The rule underneath all of it: every client is valuable, and you should keep every one of them satisfied, because you never know who they are going to refer. A family who had a good night tells their friends, and their friends live in the same neighbourhood and have the same money.
The reverse is just as true. A bad night talks too, and it talks faster.
Cold outreach that actually works
Cold messages work when they are not cold in the way most people mean.

Use their name. Spend two minutes on their page first so you can reference something real. Personal beats a blast every single time, and it is not close. Ten thoughtful messages will outperform two hundred copy pasted ones, and you will feel better sending them.

And honestly, you will get rejected. That is something you have to learn to live with and move on from. Don't think of every "no" as a failure. Think of it as another step toward the next client, another opportunity to build your confidence, and another rep at getting better at outreach.
Other chefs are not your competition
This one surprised me.

Chefs send me work and they do it because they trust my skill set and they trust that the guest is going to have a good night with me. Their reputation is riding on the handoff, so the trust has to be real.

And I send work out too whenever I cannot take a date, or when I need extra hands, I bring in people I trust. They handle prep and cooking; I handle the guest. If I cannot take a job and I have nobody to send it to, I ask to rebook rather than leave a client with nothing. Ghosting a date you cannot cover is how you lose the relationships with your client.
I have also invested in a chef who was coming up. He staged under me until he was ready, and he works with me now.

I care about that part more than the rest of this article, honestly. I came out of an industry that treats chefs as replaceable and pays them accordingly. If I have any influence over how another chef's career goes, I want to pay them well, respect them, and give them enough information to build something of their own.
The people in the house
Nannies. House managers. Personal assistants. Vendors.

You are all one operation. The house manager knows things about the schedule that you need, the nanny knows what the kids will and won't eat, and the PA knows there are four extra people coming on Friday before you do. Communicate with them and vibe with them.
If the staff side of the house goes bad, the family feels it. They may not know exactly what is wrong, but they will know the household feels tense, and eventually somebody gets blamed for it.

Suppliers deserve the same effort. Reach out, tell them you are a private chef and ask if you can work something out. Food, equipment, linen etc. Those relationships save you money and they save you on the night when you need something at short notice.
Where I fall short
I do not keep a CRM. I should.

I do not stay in touch with past clients on any real system. I am telling you this because I would rather be useful than look organized. The thing I want to build is something simple. An automated note on a client's birthday that reminds them of the last dinner I cooked for them and asks whether they want another one. Recurring clients come back far more easily when somebody reminds them that they can.
Right now the reminder does not happen, and I know there is money sitting in that gap.
Rooms worth being in
Facebook groups and Reddit threads are worth your time. Other chefs are in there, and so are people asking where to find one.

Brigade is the community I want that energy in. Restaurant chefs transitioning into private chef work, talking to each other instead of figuring it out alone. That is the whole reason I am writing any of this. When I was in a restaurant, I was thinking about how to level up in that restaurant or move to a better one. It never occurred to me that private cheffing was a door because nobody told me. I want fewer chefs to have that gap..
How you get a bad name fast
Show up late. Be disrespectful. Bring a bad attitude into a house where a family is trying to eat dinner.
Word of mouth in this industry is fast and it can genuinely hurt your business. The private world is smaller than the restaurant world.
So every time I meet a client, I put on my best self. Walk in with a smile, shake hands, greet everyone in the room. Go above and beyond in a way they notice.

That is networking. It is not just collecting contacts or sending messages. It is every relationship you build with other chefs, the staff inside the house, your suppliers, and the family you already cook for every week.

author: Jordan Chan

title: How to build a private chef resume
dek: I did not have a single day of private chef experience when I got my first private chef job.

body.text: I did not have a single day of private chef experience when I got my first private chef job.

I want to lead with that, because I know what it feels like to look at a posting, see "previous private household experience required," and close the tab. I did that for a while. Then I stopped doing it, and I found the job on Indeed, where a chef in Toronto was starting his own agency and decided to take me on.

So before you rewrite anything, understand what a private chef resume is actually for. It is not a wall of tasting menus. It is two proofs: proof that you can cook, and proof that a family can have you in their home.
What goes on the page

Write down your previous kitchen experience. All of them, honestly. For me that is the oyster boy job where I started. Chucking oysters, cooking seafood, and not much else. The restaurants in Toronto, Mississauga, and Oakville and even my internship job from culinary school.
This belongs on the page because a household still needs a chef with discipline, strong fundamentals, and the ability to execute.

Put down the experience you have that is transferrable. Shopping, menu planning. Prep. Cooking. Cleaning. Greeting the guest. That is the actual job description of a private chef, and a restaurant resume hides every bit of it, because in a restaurant other people owned those pieces.

If you have ever done a full day solo like a catering gig, a pop-up, a family event, write it in those terms. Not "cooked for 30 people." Say you planned the menu, sourced it, executed it alone, and cleaned the kitchen after.

Put down your certifications. Food safety. Food handlers. Smart Serve. Police check. A lot of houses want a contract, an NDA, and a background check, and you are often working around the kids, so the police check is standard. If you already have it in hand, say so up front. It removes friction from the hire and it signals that you understand what kind of job this is.

Put down the households, if you have them. Size matters. Mine are usually 4 to 7 people, high net worth, full-time plus events. Do not invent titles you never held. This industry is small, they verify with past employers, and getting caught is worse than having a short resume.
What the paper cannot do
The food is a big part of your resume. But the first impression when you meet the client is what actually decides it.

Can you be personable? Can you be hospitable? Can you connect with this family and vibe with them? That is what sets you apart from every other chef with a comparable background, and there are a lot of chefs with comparable backgrounds.

A stage is your live resume, and it is where the real hiring happens. Make sure you have a clean station, dishes done as you go, multitasking without looking panicked, identifying flavors out loud. You are showing the full skill set in a single afternoon, and they cannot get any of it from a PDF no matter how well formatted it is.
I also document the work and post it on social media. This is genuinely how people have contacted me for dinner parties. Whether you like it or not, that is part of your resume now.
If you have zero private chef nights, start here
This is the exact path, and it costs almost nothing.

Reach out to friends and family. Tell them you are offering private events, dinners, celebrations. Ask if anything is coming up that you could cook for. Then do the first dinner at cost, meaning all groceries paid for, labor free.

I know how that sounds. Free labor is not a business model. But this specific dinner is not a business mondel, it is your entry point, and it does four things at once. It gets you into the work. It starts your referral network. It gives you a real line on your resume that is not a restaurant. And it tells you honestly whether you actually want this life or whether you just liked the idea of it.
Then document it and post it. That is how you gather credibility, and credibility is how you get the next one.
After that first one, you charge.
What the agency route asks for

Agencies will want previous experience, a resume, and a clear answer to why you want the role. Then a call or a Zoom, background checks, then they verify with past employers. They send your packet to the house and the family interviews you, or they run a trial.
Understand their position: agencies want chefs who have already been doing this, because they are protecting their own trust and reputation with families who pay them a lot of money.

So if you do not have household experience yet, the friends and family dinners plus your social proof are what you send them instead. That is how you build your resume and the thing they are looking for.
The short version
Write the kitchens you actually worked. Write the house skills you actually have. Get the certifications. Cook one dinner for someone you love, at cost, and document it properly to show your proof.

author: Jordan Chan
